 Beyond trends: Reality check for K-beauty brands in India as market matures 
 Eshika Chopra 
 | 4 hours ago 
 Views: 513 
 Your browser does not support the audio element. 
 --> 
 K-beauty has come a long way in India. From being closely associated with 10-step routines and the larger Korean culture wave, it has now become part of the everyday beauty conversation. But as the category grows, the consumer is changing too. The curiosity around Korean products is increasingly being replaced by questions around ingredients, efficacy, value and whether a product actually earns a place in the routine. 
 That shift also comes at a time when beauty discovery itself is changing. A product can go viral overnight through a creator or social platform, but getting consumers to return to it is a different challenge. For brands, this makes the balance between excitement and credibility increasingly important. 
 --> 
 In conversation with Adgully, Mini Sood Banerjee, Deputy Director, Amorepacific Group , speaks about the evolution of K-beauty in India, what younger consumers are really looking for, and how global beauty brands can localise without losing their identity. She also discusses MAMONDE’s opportunity in India, the changing role of beauty marketing, and why the next phase of the category could be driven by trust rather than just trends.  
 K-beauty has moved from a niche trend to a mainstream beauty category in India. What is the biggest change you have seen in the Indian consumer that tells you K-beauty has truly entered its next phase?  
 I think the biggest change is that consumers are no longer discovering K-beauty just because it is Korean. Earlier, there was a lot of curiosity around Korean beauty, Korean culture and the routines themselves. Today, the conversation is much more about what a product does for your skin. 
 The Indian consumer has become far more informed. They are reading ingredients, understanding their skin concerns and comparing products before making a purchase. So, K-beauty is no longer being seen as a trend or a category that is interesting because it comes from Korea. It is increasingly being evaluated on the same parameters as any other serious skincare category efficacy, formulation, experience and value. 
 That, to me, is a strong indication that K-beauty has entered a much more mature phase in India.  
 Gen Z is driving much of the beauty conversation today, but they are also quick to move from one trend to another. What is making younger Indian consumers stay with K-beauty beyond the initial fascination with Korean culture?  
 Gen Z is definitely trend-aware, but they are also very discerning. They may discover a product through a trend or a creator, but they will stay with it only if it delivers. 
 What works in K-beauty is that it brings together sensoriality, innovation and a strong focus on skin health. Younger consumers are also much more comfortable experimenting with their routines and understanding ingredients. They want products that fit into their lifestyle and solve a specific need rather than simply adding another product to their shelf. 
 For us, the opportunity is to make that discovery meaningful. With MAMONDE, for instance, we are bringing Korean formulation expertise and innovation in a way that feels accessible and relevant to a younger Indian consumer.  
 Indian consumers are becoming more ingredient-conscious, efficacy-led and value-conscious at the same time. How is this combination changing the way premium and mass-premium beauty brands need to build their propositions?  
 Consumers today are asking a very simple question: “What am I getting for what I am paying?” 
 Premiumisation can no longer be built only around packaging, heritage or aspiration. There has to be a clear reason for the consumer to believe in the product whether that is the ingredients, the technology, the formulation or the results. 
 At the same time, being efficacy-led does not mean the proposition has to become complicated. Consumers appreciate brands that can communicate the benefit clearly and honestly. I think the brands that will win are the ones that can bring together strong product credentials with accessibility and a very clear consumer proposition.  
 The original K-beauty appeal was often associated with elaborate routines and multiple products. Today, consumers are talking more about skin barriers, targeted solutions and simpler routines. Is K-beauty itself having to rethink the multi-step skincare philosophy?  
 I would say K-beauty has always been about understanding the skin rather than simply following a fixed number of steps. The multi-step routine became the most visible representation of K-beauty, but the philosophy itself has evolved. 
 Today, consumers are more aware of what their skin actually needs. They may still enjoy layering products, but they are more selective about why they are using each product. There is a clear shift towards targeted solutions, barrier care and products that can deliver multiple benefits without making the routine unnecessarily complicated. 
 So, I don't see it as K-beauty moving away from its philosophy. I see it as K-beauty evolving with the consumer.  
 Indian skincare brands have become much stronger competitors, particularly on ingredients, affordability and local consumer understanding. Where do you think Indian brands currently have an edge over global K-beauty players, and where do global brands still have an advantage?  
 Indian brands have a very strong understanding of the local consumer. They are close to the market; they understand Indian skin concerns, price sensitivities and the way consumers shop here. That agility is a real advantage. 
 Where global K-beauty brands can bring something different is in the depth of R&D, formulation expertise and the innovation ecosystem that has been built in Korea over many years. Korea has a very dynamic beauty market, where consumers are highly engaged, and brands are constantly innovating. 
 I don't necessarily see it as Indian versus Korean brands. I think the Indian market is big enough for brands to bring different strengths to the table, and ultimately the consumer decides based on what works best for them.  
 How far can a global beauty brand localise in India without losing the identity that made it successful globally? What aspects of the Indian market do you believe require the most localisation?  
 For me, localisation is not about changing the DNA of the brand. It is about understanding how that DNA can become relevant to the Indian consumer. 
 You need to retain what makes the brand distinctive its philosophy, formulation expertise, innovation and visual identity while being flexible about how you communicate and build the business in a particular market. 
 In India, understanding the consumer, the climate, the way people shop, the price-value equation and the platforms through which they discover beauty is extremely important. Even the way we educate consumers about a product has to be culturally relevant. 
 The brand should still feel unmistakably itself, but the consumer should also feel that it understands them.  
 MAMONDE is being positioned as a more accessible, Gen Z-focused K-beauty brand. What gap in the Indian beauty market did you see that led Amorepacific to bring MAMONDE to India now?  
 We saw an opportunity for a brand that could bring the credibility of Korean beauty innovation to a younger consumer in a way that felt approachable and relevant. 
 MAMONDE has a strong heritage of botanical expertise and innovation, but it also has a very contemporary way of looking at beauty. The brand is about discovering the power of flowers and translating that into modern skincare. 
 India's younger consumers are already very familiar with K-beauty. So the opportunity now is not simply to introduce them to Korean beauty, but to give them products and experiences that they can genuinely incorporate into their everyday routines. 
 That is where MAMONDE fits in. It brings Amorepacific's Korean beauty expertise together with a more accessible and contemporary proposition.  
 Beauty discovery is increasingly happening through creators, reviews, communities and platforms such as Nykaa. Has the role of marketing changed from creating aspiration to building trust and educating consumers?  
 Definitely. Aspiration will always have a role in beauty, but today it has to be supported by credibility. 
 Consumers have access to so much information that brands cannot simply tell them that a product is good. They want to understand why it is good, what it does and whether it is right for their skin. 
 Creators and communities have also changed the conversation because consumers now hear from people who are actually using the products. For us, marketing is therefore becoming much more about education, transparency and creating the right context around the product. 
 Platforms like Nykaa are important in that journey because discovery and purchase can happen almost simultaneously. That makes it even more important for the consumer to have the right information at the point of consideration.  
 There is also some fatigue around viral beauty products and influencer-led recommendations, with consumers increasingly asking whether a product actually works. Is the next phase of beauty marketing going to be less about hype and more about demonstrating efficacy?  
 I think we are already seeing that shift. Virality can create awareness, but it cannot necessarily create long-term loyalty. A product may become popular overnight, but if consumers don't see a reason to repurchase it, the momentum doesn't sustain. 
 The next phase of beauty marketing will be much more balanced. Brands will still need to create excitement, but they will also have to substantiate the excitement with a strong product story, ingredients, formulation, technology and, most importantly, the consumer experience. 
 Ultimately, the best marketing for a beauty product is still a product that works and a consumer who comes back to it.  
 Looking three to five years ahead, what is the opportunity in Indian beauty that you think the industry is currently underestimating?  
 The biggest opportunity is the evolution of the Indian consumer. 
 We often talk about India as a large market, but what is more interesting is how quickly consumers are becoming more sophisticated. They are experimenting more, understanding ingredients better and expecting greater transparency from brands. 
 I also think there is a significant opportunity beyond the metros. As beauty knowledge and digital discovery continue to spread, consumers in smaller cities and towns will become an increasingly important part of the premium and masstige beauty market. 
 For brands, the opportunity is not just to sell more products. It is to build long-term relationships with consumers by understanding what they need at different stages of their beauty journey. 
 That is where I think the next phase of growth will come from: moving from simply creating products for consumers to building brands that consumers genuinely trust and want to stay with.
